stem: A freely filtered experimental marker initially appears in urine at exactly its filtered rate. A transporter is then activated that returns some filtered marker from the tubule to the body. Its plasma concentration and true filtration remain constant. Which of the following best describes a filtration estimate based on urinary marker appearance?

options.text: It becomes too high because tubular recovery adds marker
options.explanation: Recovery from the tubular fluid reduces rather than adds to the urinary marker amount. An upward bias would instead require an additional route into urine.
options.label: A
options.misconception: Treats recovery from the tubule as addition to urinary marker appearance.

options.text: It remains accurate because plasma concentration is constant
options.explanation: A constant plasma concentration does not correct altered tubular handling. The urinary numerator now excludes recovered marker, so it no longer represents the full filtered amount.
options.label: B
options.misconception: Assumes a constant plasma denominator corrects a urinary numerator altered by tubular recovery.

options.text: It becomes too high because secretion raises urinary appearance
options.explanation: Secretion would add marker to urine, but the intervention moves marker in the opposite direction. The described transporter produces urinary subtraction and a lower estimate.
options.label: C
options.misconception: Confuses return of filtered marker to the body with secretion of additional marker into urine.

options.text: It remains accurate because secretion has not been introduced
options.explanation: Avoiding secretion is insufficient if reabsorption occurs. Both processes must be absent for urinary marker appearance to equal the filtered amount in this measurement design.
options.label: D
options.misconception: Assumes absence of secretion is sufficient for an accurate estimate even when reabsorption occurs.

options.text: It becomes too low because tubular recovery removes marker
options.explanation: Returning filtered marker to the body subtracts from its urinary appearance. The resulting estimate undercounts the filtered amount despite unchanged plasma concentration and true filtration.
options.label: E
options.misconception: No misconception: tubular recovery subtracts from urinary marker appearance and underestimates filtration.

context: Learning objective: Explain downward bias introduced when a filtration marker is reabsorbed. Returning filtered marker to the body subtracts from its urinary appearance. The resulting estimate undercounts the filtered amount despite unchanged plasma concentration and true filtration.
